It is also recognized that operational changes as described above would not be realized for less-than-truckload shipments, inasmuch as these shipments would more than likely continue to be broken down at terminal facilities and peddled to plantsites by local carriers. Furthermore, union rules may require the driver of a line haul truck to drive only from terminal to terminal. It is not possible to predict how these offsetting factors will effect the environmental benefits anticipated from a decrease in interlining. It should be noted, however, that the Federal action being taken in this proceeding will enable carriers to operate more efficiently by eliminating certain interline practices as appropriate. By affording carriers this opportunity, the Commission is taking an action which has the potential for a degree of environmental benefit. But it is not possible to predict the extent to which carriers will avail themselves of this opportunity.
To the extent that certain interline practices are eliminated, this action is consistent with the goals and policies established by the Clean Air Act of 1970. This act requires all States to submit plans for meeting the national ambient air quality standards established by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1971. The standards are directed towards protecting the public health and welfare from known effects of the major air pollutants, including the four primary ones associated with motor vehicles: carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide, photo-chemical oxidant, and hydrocarbons. Transportation control plans (TCP) are required for any air quality region where controls on stationary sources, combined with Federal new car emission standards, are inadequate to ensure attainment or maintenance of the ambient standards. TCP's have been generally required for major metropolitan areas which typically exhibit high concentrations of air pollutants.
